Colorectal cancer The findings of this review show that DMC for colorectal cancer encompass various healthcare resource utilization or cost items, including specialist visits, inpatient hospital care (such as the costs of inpatient drugs, nursing care, and use of inpatient resources), diagnostic services, surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, rehabilitation such as physiotherapy, as well as medication and drugs. The costs of diagnostic services include laboratory tests, pathology, computed tomography scan (CT scan), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasonography, electrocardiography, electroencephalography, radiography, nuclear medicine, endoscopy, and other diagnostic laboratory and radiology services [ 23 – 26 ] (Table 2 ). In Jafari et al.’s study, the average DMC per colorectal cancer patient in 2019 were estimated to be $4,301 (1 USD = 42,000 IRR) [ 23 ]. In Nejati et al.’s study, these costs for 2016 were equivalent to $17,038 (1 USD = 8,212.15 IRR) [ 24 ], and in Vahdatimanesh et al.’s study for 2012 and in Davari et al.’s study for 2011, the costs were equivalent to $4,242 (1 USD = 12,229 IRR) and $7,768 (1 USD = 10,965 IRR), respectively [ 25 , 26 ]. Additionally, Jafari et al. estimated the total costs for colorectal cancer in 2019 to be $46 million for the whole country. In the study by Vahdatimanesh et al. in 2012, these total costs were estimated at $96 million (Table 3 ). Converting the costs to USD 2021 showed that the average DMC per patient with colorectal cancer in different studies varied from $14,671 to $28,656 (mean = $20,840; median = $20,016) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average DNMC per colorectal cancer patient in Jafari et al.’s study, taking into account the costs of accommodation, transportation of patients and companions, food for the patient and companions, special diet, changing the home environment to adapt to the disease, telephone and internet calls to family, babysitters and kindergartens, and purchase of aids, were estimated at $949 in 2019 [ 23 ]. These costs were estimated to be $4,388 in 2016 in the study by Nejati et al., who included the costs of guardian services and hoteling as DNMC [ 24 ]. In Vahdatimanesh et al.’s study in 2012, the costs were approximately $1,297, considering the costs of patient time and transportation as DNMC [ 25 ]. Jafari et al. estimated these costs for the whole country to be $10 million, while Vahdatimanesh et al. estimated them at $29 million (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average DNMC per colorectal cancer patient in these studies varied from $3,526 to $6,193 (mean = $4,735; median= $4,485) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average IDC per colorectal cancer patient in the study by Jafari et al. in 2019 were estimated to be $495 [ 23 ]. In Vahdatimanesh et al.’s study, these costs were estimated to be approximately $7,659 per patient and $173 million for the whole country in 2012 [ 25 ]. In Jafari et al.’s study, these costs only included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and their companions, whereas in Vahdatimanesh et al.’s study, these costs only included the costs of lost productivity due to premature death (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average IDC per colorectal cancer patient in these two studies were $1,841 and $26,490, respectively (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). Prostate cancer The findings of this review show that DMC for prostate cancer encompass various healthcare resource utilization or cost items, including specialist visits, hospitalization, diagnostic services (such as imaging and cystoscopy, laboratory and pathology services), surgery (including radical prostatectomy and orchiectomy surgery), radiotherapy, chemotherapy, hormone therapy, rehabilitation, as well as medication and drugs (such as antiandrogens and luteinizing hormone agonists) [ 27 – 29 ] (Table 2 ). In Alinezhad et al.’s study, the average DMC per prostate cancer patient in 2018 were estimated to be $3,773 PPP (exchange rate not reported) [ 27 ]. In Foroughi Moghadam et al.’s study, these costs for 2015 were equivalent to $2,934 (1 USD = 29,580 IRR) [ 28 ]. Mojahidian et al.’s study in 2016 reported these costs by different disease states, ranging from $103 for low-risk metastatic prostate cancer to $7,748 for resistant metastatic prostate cancer (exchange rate not reported) [ 29 ]. The DMC of prostate cancer for the whole country were estimated at $2 million in Alinezhad et al.’s study and $12.5 million in Foroughi Moghadam et al.’s study (Table 3 ). Converting the costs to USD 2021 showed that the average DMC per patient with prostate cancer in different studies varied from $7,970 to $16,821 (mean = $13,704; median = $16,320) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average DNMC per prostate cancer patient in Alinezhad et al.’s study, taking into account the costs of transportation, accommodation, and a disease-specific diet in 2018, were estimated to be $186 PPP [ 27 ]. In the study by Mojahidian et al., these costs, considering the costs of intra-city and inter-city travel to receive services, hotel accommodation, and food consumed during the trip in 2016, varied from $97 for low-risk metastatic prostate cancer to $1,068 for resistant metastatic prostate cancer [ 29 ]. In the study by Foroughi Moghadam et al., these costs were estimated to be approximately $200 per patient and $898 thousand for the whole country based on the new cases identified in 2015, considering the costs of transportation and accommodation as DNMC [ 28 ] (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average DNMC per prostate cancer patient in these studies varied from $300 to $2,652 (mean = $1,374; median = $1,171) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average IDC per prostate cancer patient in the study by Alinezhad et al. in 2018 were estimated to be $1,307 PPP [ 27 ]. These costs varied based on different disease states and were reported in the study by Mojahidian et al. in 2016, ranging from $24 for low-risk metastatic prostate cancer to $358 for resistant metastatic prostate cancer [ 29 ]. In the study by Foroughi Moghadam et al., these costs were estimated to be approximately $2,920 per patient and $12 million for the whole country, based on the new cases identified in 2015 [ 28 ]. Alinezhad et al. included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and their companions, as well as the costs of lost productivity due to premature death. However, in the studies by Mojahidian et al. and Foroughi Moghadam et al., these costs only included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and the patient’s family (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average IDC per prostate cancer patient in these three studies were $10,857, $739, and $16,239, respectively (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). Gastric cancer The findings of this review show that DMC for gastric cancer encompass various healthcare resource utilization or cost items, including specialist visits, hospitalization, diagnostic services (such as initial tests, pre-chemotherapy tests, follow-up tests, CT scan, MRI, ultrasonography, endoscopy, colonoscopy, and other diagnostic laboratory and radiology services), surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, as well as medication and drugs (including the costs of chemotherapy drugs, supportive drugs) [ 30 – 32 ] (Table 2 ). In the study by Jalilian et al., the average DMC per gastric cancer patient in 2017 were estimated to be $3,288 (1 USD = 32,441 IRR) [ 30 ]. In the study by Eghdami et al., these costs for 2016 were equivalent to $2,350 (1 USD = 30,221 IRR) [ 31 ]. In the study by Izadi et al., these costs in 2015 were estimated to be 113,370,129 Rials for the private sector and 74,705,158 Rials for the public sector [ 32 ] (Table 3 ). Converting the costs to USD 2021 showed that the average DMC per patient with gastric cancer in different studies varied from $12,206 to $17,681 (mean = $15,369; median = $16,220) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average DNMC per gastric cancer patient in Jalilian et al.’s study, taking into account the costs of travel, accommodation, and food in 2017, were estimated to be $378 [ 30 ]. In the study by Eghdami et al., these costs were equal to $522 for 2016, considering the costs of transportation, accommodation, food for the patient and relatives, the patient’s consumables, and the accommodation of the people who visit the patient at his, her home [ 31 ] (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average DNMC per gastric cancer patient in these studies varied from $1,862 to $2,711 (mean = median = $2,287) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average IDC per gastric cancer patient in the study by Jalilian et al. in 2017 were estimated to be $505 [ 30 ]. I In the study by Eghdami et al., these costs for 2016 were equal to $1,094 [ 31 ]. Both studies included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and the patient’s companions (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average IDC per gastric cancer patient in these two studies were $2,493 and $5,682, respectively (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). Lung cancer The findings of this review show that DMC for lung cancer encompass various healthcare resource utilization or cost items, including specialist visits, hospitalization, diagnostic services, surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, physiotherapy, as well as medication and drugs [ 33 – 35 ] (Table 2 ). In Mir et al.’s study, the average DMC per lung cancer patient in 2016 were estimated to be $7,542 (exchange rate not reported) [ 33 ]. In Mohagheghi et al.’s study, these costs for 2009 were equivalent to $1,932 (1 USD = 9,917 IRR) [ 35 ]. Additionally, Mohagheghi et al. estimated the total costs for lung cancer in 2009 to be $11 million for the whole country based on the incidence of the disease. In Rezaei et al.’s study, these total costs were estimated to be 350 billion Rials for the whole country based on the 5-year prevalence of the disease in 2014 [ 34 ] (Table 3 ). Converting the costs to USD 2021 showed that the average DMC per patient with lung cancer in different studies varied from $9,369 to $40,682 (mean = $21,280; median = $13,785) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). In the study by Mir et al., the average DNMC per lung cancer patient in 2016, taking into account the costs of transportation, food, and accommodation, were estimated to be $499 [ 33 ]. In the study by Rezaei et al., these costs, considering transportation, accommodation, food, care for family members such as the elderly or children, and other service costs such as telephone bills for the whole country based on the 5-year prevalence of the disease in 2014, were estimated at 87 billion Rials [ 34 ] (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average DNMC per lung cancer patient in these studies varied from $2,690 to $3,428 (mean = median = $3,059) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average IDC per lung cancer patient in the study by Mir et al. in 2017 were estimated to be $11,903 [ 33 ]. In the study by Rezaei et al., these costs for the whole country were estimated to be approximately 584 million Rials per patient and 2,789 billion Rials based on the 5-year prevalence of the disease in 2014 [ 34 ]. Both studies included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and their companions, as well as the costs of lost productivity due to premature death (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average IDC per lung cancer patient in these two studies were $64,207 and $110,015, respectively (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average IDC per lung cancer patient in the study by Mir et al. in 2017 were estimated to be $11,903 [ 33 ]. In the study by Rezaei et al., these costs for the whole country were estimated to be approximately 584 million Rials per patient and 2,789 billion Rials based on the 5-year prevalence of the disease in 2014 [ 34 ]. Both studies included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and their companions, as well as the costs of lost productivity due to premature death (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average IDC per lung cancer patient in these two studies were $64,207 and $110,015, respectively (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). Discussion As the findings indicate, the healthcare resource utilization or cost items for DMC may vary depending on the type of cancer, while the cost items for DNMC and IDC are similar for all cancers. Most of the differences among cost items for DMC are linked to diagnostic services. For instance, one of the cost items for breast cancer that other cancers do not have is the diagnostic cost of mammography. Similarly, one of the cost items for colorectal cancer that other cancers do not have is the diagnostic cost of colonoscopy. This highlights the importance of recognizing the unique cost drivers for each cancer type in healthcare planning, as they contribute significantly to the overall economic burden. Converting the costs from different studies to USD 2021 showed that the average annual DMC per patient with breast cancer in Iran varied from $13,954 to $34,772 [ 19 – 22 ]. These costs range from $14,671 to $28,656 for colorectal cancer [ 23 – 26 ], $7,970 to $16,821 for prostate cancer [ 27 – 29 ], $12,206 to $17,681 for gastric cancer [ 30 – 32 ], and $9,369 to $40,682 for lung cancer [ 33 – 35 ]. Part of this variation is related to the different healthcare resource utilization or cost items considered for cost calculation. Another part may be due to differences in cost calculation methodology, study perspective, and study location (private or public sector). The observed cost variation reflects the complex interplay of healthcare policies, resource availability, and methodological choices across different studies. Since these five cancers are the most common cancers in Iran, multiplying these costs by the total number of people with cancer makes the total cost for the country significant. For example, in the study by Daroudi et al. in 2010, the costs for breast cancer in the whole country were estimated at $176 million [ 21 ]. Therefore, the researchers emphasize that the disease burden is one dimension of the problem, and the other dimension is the economic burden of the disease, which, if not addressed, can have significant effects on the country’s health economics. Without targeted policies to reduce diagnostic and treatment costs, this economic pressure may challenge the sustainability of Iran’s healthcare system. The cost items for DNMC are similar across all cancers. These items include the costs of accommodation, transportation for patients and companions (both intra-city and inter-city), food for patients and companions, special diets, telephone and internet communication with family, purchasing auxiliary equipment, patient consumables, modifying the home environment to adapt to the disease, childcare, eldercare, kindergarten services, hiring a housemaid, and accommodating visitors at the patient’s home [ 19 – 21 , 23 – 25 , 27 – 31 , 33 , 34 ]. However, due to limitations in measuring these costs, some cost items might be ignored or simpler methods might be used to measure them. Ignoring certain DNMC items may lead to an underestimation of the total economic burden, especially in cases where these costs are substantial, potentially resulting in insufficient resource allocation and inadequate support for patients and their families. Based on USD 2021, in 85% of studies (11 out of 13 studies), the average annual DNMC per patient are estimated to be less than $4,000 for each patient suffering from one of these five cancers [ 19 – 21 , 23 , 27 – 31 , 33 , 34 ]. In other studies, (2 out of 13 studies), these costs were more than $4,000 that were related to colorectal cancer [ 24 , 25 ]. This finding suggests that DNMC, though generally lower than DMC, still represent a significant burden, particularly for cancers like colorectal cancer where these costs exceed $4,000, underscoring the need for comprehensive support systems for cancer patients and their families. The authors believe that the similarity in DNMC across cancers reflects broader socioeconomic impacts on patients and their families, highlighting the need for universal support services that address non-medical costs among cancer patients. IDC, like DNMC, have similar cost items across all cancers. These items include the costs of lost productivity due to the patient’s absence from work, the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient’s companions who care for them, and the costs of lost productivity due to premature death [ 19 – 21 , 23 – 25 , 27 – 31 , 33 , 34 ]. It is important to consider that due to limitations in measurement, some of these cost items may be ignored in studies, or they may be measured based on assumptions. Since the death and disability rate is much higher in some cancers compared to others, the variance of these costs may be significant among different cancers. For instance, based on USD 2021, the average annual IDC per patient with breast and lung cancer, due to high mortality, were approximately $100,000 [ 34 ], while for other cancers, the average annual IDC were less than $30,000 [ 25 , 27 ]. The researchers conclude that the high IDC associated with cancers like breast and lung cancer, driven by high mortality rates, calls for more preventive and early detection programs to reduce productivity loss. Focusing on these high-mortality cancers could further help alleviate both individual and national economic burdens. Given the complexity of measuring, future research could focus on refining cost measurement techniques, particularly for DNMC and IDC, and addressing methodological differences across studies. Additionally, exploring how integrating cancer support services, such as palliative care, psychological support, and family care, might reduce some of these non-medical and indirect costs would be valuable. Limitations Since this review is related to Iran and almost all studies from this country have been published in Persian and English, we did not face significant language limitations. However, since most of the studies focus on specific regions or healthcare settings within Iran, the findings may not be fully generalizable to all regions or healthcare environments in the country. Additionally, due to the nature of the search strategy and the selected databases, there is always the possibility of missing studies in a systematic review. To reduce this limitation, we developed a detailed search strategy and selected diverse databases. Finally, due to the heterogeneous nature of cost definitions and measurements among the included studies in this review, comparing costs across studies was difficult. Therefore, in the study findings section, efforts were made to compare costs more cautiously, and for this purpose, the findings have been reported in more detail. Conclusion Cancer encompasses a wide range of resources and cost items. For researchers to accurately examine DMC, DNMC, and IDC in future studies, they should aim to include all or at least most of these cost items in their calculations. Despite the limitations in calculating some of these costs, findings from studies indicate that the costs associated with the five most common cancers in Iran are significant. Therefore, efforts by policymakers to combat cancer should not only focus on reducing the burden of the disease but also aim to alleviate the economic burden it imposes. To achieve this, policymakers could consider implementing more efficient resource allocation strategies, enhancing access to early detection and preventive programs, and investing in cost-effective treatment protocols. Additionally, establishing financial support systems for patients, particularly for non-medical costs, could mitigate the economic challenges faced by cancer patients and their families.
